band_note: Frequency B (5 MHz, natively 80 m) was used. It is the same acquisition and geometry as the 20 MHz frequency A band at 1/16 the data volume; measured dB percentiles agree with frequency A to within a few tenths of a dB. Costs: more speckle, and NISAR's known-issues page reports larger systematic radiometric calibration residuals for frequency B than for frequency A.

despeckle.method: Multitemporal speckle filter (Quegan & Yu 2001), 5x5 local window, over all 10 dates; then classified pixels with no same-class neighbour are removed.
despeckle.why: Radar images are grainy (speckle). Unfiltered, about one in six mapped pixels stood alone, which is noise, not ponds. The filter uses the other dates to clean each date without blurring thin channels.
despeckle.effect: Mapped areas are smaller than unfiltered ones. The dates of the two seasonal peaks do not change.
despeckle.note: class.png and timeseries.json are filtered; hh.png is the unfiltered radar image.

geometry.note: All dates share one track/frame/pass, so differences between dates are real surface change and not a change in viewing geometry.

gap_note: NISAR has a permanent data gap in this window. Show it as 'no data', not as 'no flood'.
uncertainty_note: Backscatter thresholds are fixed, physically motivated values, identical on every date. They are not calibrated against ground measurements, so treat the areas as a consistent relative index of flooding rather than an absolute hydrological measurement.
conservative_note: These thresholds are deliberately strict, so the mapped area is a lower bound. Published estimates of the Okavango's total seasonal flood extent are several times larger; part of that difference is real (the area of interest and one radar frame do not cover the whole delta) and part is the strict thresholds. The shape of the seasonal curve is more reliable than its absolute level.
quality_note: Dates up to 2026-10-12 are NISAR PROVISIONAL products; 2026-10-24 is VALIDATED. A small calibration offset between the two is possible.

legend.label: Open water
legend.why: Calm water mirrors the radar pulse away, so very little energy returns: HH is very low.

legend.label: Flooded vegetation
legend.why: The pulse bounces off the water and then off trunks and stems and returns to the radar (double bounce): HH is very high and much higher than HV. L-band sees this under the canopy; C-band largely cannot.
